entry.content:

François Chatelain, working as F&C ai Lab, gives a familiar piece of design-world placeholder text its own hip-hop video. Lorem Ipsum Rap builds an AI-generated animated clip around “Lorem Ipsum / Dolor Sit Amet,” turning words usually left in the background into the song’s central hook.

The visual language is equally emphatic: saturated yellow, orange and pink, graffiti-like marks, oversized lettering and illustrated performers. Typography becomes part of the imagery, filling the title, wrapping across a pair of lips and appearing as gold rings on a rapper’s hands. The supplied frames carry an explicit AI mark.

Chatelain made the project solo, using AI across the music, imagery, animated sequences and editing. His production notes identify Suno for the music, Midjourney for the visual style and illustrations, and Seedance for the animated sequences. ChatGPT assisted with the concept, prompts and creative direction.

The result brings the language of graphic layouts into a music-video setting, giving placeholder copy a voice and a vivid visual identity. See more of Chatelain’s experiments in his AI video portfolio.

entry.title: The Flowers Look Back: teamLab at OFFF Barcelona 2026
entry.summary: Editor’s note: Our OFFF Barcelona 2026 conversations continue. Following Onur Senturk on the compulsion to create , Tim Thompson of RevThink sits down with Sakurako “Saka” Naka of teamLab, the Tokyo art collective behind Borderless and Phenomena, the morning after her talk on the...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s note: Our OFFF Barcelona 2026 conversations continue. Following Onur Senturk on the compulsion to create, Tim Thompson of RevThink sits down with Sakurako “Saka” Naka of teamLab, the Tokyo art collective behind Borderless and Phenomena, the morning after her talk on the main stage. What follows is Tim’s account of the conversation.

Saka arrived with a laptop and an apology. “I didn’t prepare myself at all,” she said, “because I think it’s very uninteresting, for the most part.” We were outside Disseny Hub on the last morning of the festival, in the sun, a few hours before she had to be back on a plane to Tokyo. By the time an OFFF producer came to find her, nearly an hour later, I had stopped asking questions and she had stopped apologizing.

I came to the conversation wanting to understand a structure. How does an art collective become big enough to open permanent museums on three continents without turning into a company, or at least without feeling like one? I left with something closer to a philosophy of making, and with a standing invitation to Tokyo that I intend to use.

teamLab, Universe of Water Particles on a Rock where People Gather. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

A laboratory for a team

The story begins about 25 years ago with five friends leaving graduate school. One of them, Toshiyuki Inoko, whom everyone at teamLab calls Toshi, wanted to make things. “Art 25 years ago is not sustainable,” Saka said, then caught herself. “It’s not even now.” So by day the five built technology for companies, and whatever revenue came in went into artworks. “That’s how we self-sustained.”

That arrangement never went away. It grew into two pillars. One side, which they call digital solutions, builds apps and systems for postal services, banks, and airlines, and now works at a nationwide scale in Japan. The other side is the art collective. Three of the four friends who started with Toshi are still there, and they run the digital solutions side “so that Toshi can just focus on making things.”

The name is literal. “When teamLab started, the reason why it’s called teamLab is, it’s a laboratory for a team.” I asked whether that made the team the experiment. She laughed. “Not necessarily a human experiment.”

Nobody has a title

I tried to find the org chart and could not. When I asked whether Toshi functioned as a creative director, Saka paused over the comparison. “I honestly don’t know what creative directors are. We don’t have titles within teamLab.” What they have instead is what she calls a gathering of specialists. Artists, but also mathematicians, software and hardware engineers, architects, and a botanical team. “Are you serious?” I asked. She was. They work with living flowers.

Work forms around an artwork, not around a department. An idea begins, often with Toshi, and the group that gathers around it evolves by need: which specialty is required to make this, who should be experimenting on it. Some of those series have been running for more than 15 years, each iteration asking the same question in a new form, such as whether light can become a three-dimensional sculpture in space. “We’re always interested in just keeping on making,” she said. An exhibition is the moment to ask what the team is interested in right now, and what it wants to show.

When a museum or exhibition approaches, a different kind of member steps in. “We have these members called catalysts,” she said. “They bring everyone together.” I pointed out that this sounded like a title. “It’s more of an adjective.” The catalyst knows every engineer and architect working on every artwork and pulls them into the plan for the larger space.

“We don’t have titles within teamLab.”

Everyone is full time. “It’s not a drop-in, drop-out situation, because there’s always something to be making.” And the wall between the two pillars is porous. If an artwork needs an insight that lives on the digital solutions side, someone walks over. “People make friends.”

teamLab Borderless, MORI Building Digital Art Museum, Azabudai Hills, Tokyo. © teamLab

Every piece of wood is different

teamLab does everything in-house, from the first experiment to the last projector. Artworks start small in the Tokyo studio, scale up in large warehouses far outside the city, and get finished on site, where the team spends weeks working out corners and angles. “There’s so much you discover just using your hands to do things,” Saka said. “You never really know until you’re physically in the space.”

The discovery does not stay with one person. It is shared across the team and carried into the next artwork, so the knowledge compounds. Her example for this had nothing to do with projectors. In old Japanese architecture, she said, the craftsmen who shaved the wooden beams for the great temples were also part of deciding what the structure would look like. “Every piece of wood is different. So the people working with the actual material could also have an input in the larger structure.” That separation came later. “It’s not whether it’s good or bad. It’s just something different that has happened.”

The Tokyo studio is built to keep that input flowing. One floor is entirely open, a lot of tables and no walls, with only two glassed rooms so that overseas calls are possible. Everyone is working on several things at once, so when a question about a space comes up in a meeting, the person who can answer it is usually within reach. “You can tap someone over very easily.”

Somewhere in here I offered her my starfish metaphor, the one about a creature with no brain whose parts still agree on a direction, and how a whole school of them will move together with no visible way of communicating. She was polite about it. “In some of our artworks there are schools of fish. Or birds. It’s some communication that we don’t fully understand. There’s so much that we don’t know.”

The flowers look back

Then she opened the laptop, and the conversation stopped being about structure.

She showed me the garden first. More than 13,000 living orchids fill a room in Tokyo, suspended in the air with no soil, because most orchids can absorb water from the air. “They found another way to live on this planet,” she said. When you walk in, the flowers hang low. Stand still, and the ones around you begin to float upward, opening a space around your body. Walk slowly and the space moves with you. If someone enters from the other side, your two spaces merge.

teamLab, Floating Flower Garden: Flowers and I are of the Same Root, the Garden and I are One, 2015-, interactive installation. © teamLab

The work comes from a Zen saying about looking at a flower as though looking at a dream. “We know in our brains that we’re connected to nature,” she said. “But it’s difficult to recognize it as that.” The orchids are the attempt. “If you stand for a while, the flowers almost look back at you.”

“If you stand for a while, the flowers almost look back at you.”

teamLab, Floating Flower Garden. More than 13,000 living orchids, rooted in air. © teamLab

You cannot put a whirlpool in a box

Earlier I had given her a theory of mine about the four stages of a creative career, which ends with the collector, the person whose value lies in what they gather. Saka came back to it an hour later with a better answer than mine, and it started with a whirlpool.

Humans, she said, have mostly made objects. Our cities are full of them. But in the south of Japan, where Toshi grew up, there are some of the largest whirlpools in the world, and a whirlpool is not an object. The water inside it is exactly the same as the water outside it. What makes it exist is an order of energy, a flow passing through. “You could not scoop it up and put it in a silver box. It would stop existing the moment you tried.”

teamLab, Light Vortex. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi. © teamLab

That idea became a series called Environmental Phenomena, and a building. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, developed with the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi and Miral, is full of sculptures that are made by the environment itself: a column of spheres that rises about five meters and reads as a solid vertical form from across the room, held up by nothing but air flow. You can walk into it and it keeps existing. You cannot take it home. “It’s inseparable from the environment,” Saka said. “As long as this environment exists, these sculptures will continue to emerge.” I asked who at teamLab commissioned the content. “We decided everything that went in there.”

teamLab, Morphing Continuum. A sculpture of spheres held in place by the flow of air alone. teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi. © teamLab

No map

Borderless, teamLab’s permanent museum in Tokyo, moved into a new space in 2024, and the next one is going to Hamburg. There is no map and no route. You walk in and out of rooms and stay as long as you like, and the artworks do the same. They leave one room, travel the corridors, take another form, and overlap with each other. They also respond to whoever is there. The butterflies are born from people, so at the start of the day, before anyone arrives, there are no butterflies. Touch one and it dies. “It’s just one world,” she said, “and it depends on who’s there with you and how they’re behaving.”

teamLab, Flutter of Butterflies Beyond Borders. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

This is where she talked about beauty, and it is the line I keep returning to. People usually call something beautiful when it has been separated from the rest of the world, a single flower, a single ring. Inside Borderless, where everything is changing because of you and because of the strangers beside you, that reflex falls away. “At one point you start to feel like it’s the whole that’s beautiful. The fact that the world is continuous, and that we live in this continuity, that’s the object of beauty.”

“The fact that the world is continuous, and that we live in this continuity, that’s the object of beauty.”

I thought of a field of poppies. You can photograph it, or pick one flower and carry it home, and either might be lovely on its own. Neither is the field. The field includes its scale, its surroundings, and the fact that you were standing in it.

A different way of seeing

The last thing she showed me was a wall of blooming flowers, and the hardest idea of the hour. Most of what we look at now has passed through a lens, and a lens fixes a point of view. “When your perspective is fixed, you don’t need your body,” she said. That is not a bad thing, she was careful to add. It made objectivity possible. But teamLab has spent years on the opposite problem: how to turn something three-dimensional into two dimensions without discarding the body, so that what you see feels like it shares your space.

teamLab, People Don’t See the World as through a Camera. The letters at the entrance of teamLab Borderless only rise toward you through a lens. © teamLab

They call the answer Ultrasubjective Space, a logical construct for flattening a scene without fixing the viewer’s eye. In the room, you cannot tell whether the flowers are blooming on your side of the wall or beyond it, and people drift toward them without deciding to. I kept asking about the mechanism, whether there were layered planes, whether something moved. She kept returning me to how the image was built. “People don’t look at the world like a lens does in the first place.” Pre-modern East Asian scrolls and folding screens, she pointed out, were never drawn in Western perspective. “It’s probably just how they saw.” When I asked whether this was a technical breakthrough or a creative one, she gave the most teamLab answer of the morning. “Sometimes things just don’t exist, and we just have to make it up.”

teamLab, Flowers and People, Cannot be Controlled but Live Together. teamLab Borderless, Tokyo. © teamLab

Today, then tomorrow

I spend my working life with creative business owners, and most of them are being taught, including by the speakers at this festival, how to become commercial artists. teamLab did it the other way around. They built a commercial engine so the art would never have to ask permission, and 25 years later the engine is still running and the art is still the point.

People ask Toshi about his plans in five years, in ten. Saka says the answer never changes. “I just want to keep making something today. And then tomorrow, and the day after, and I’ll just keep doing that.” She smiled. “And then one day I’ll die.”

That sounds like a plan. The OFFF film crew came for her a minute later. She gave me her number for Tokyo, and I have never been to Tokyo. She is going to be the reason.

“I just want to keep making something today. And then tomorrow, and the day after.”

teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, Saadiyat Cultural District. © teamLab

Interview and words: Tim Thompson, RevThink, recorded at OFFF Barcelona 2026

entry.title: Sekondo Puts ChatGPT and Claude Inside After Effects and Premiere Pro.
entry.summary: Córdoba-based graphic designer Jose Manuel Fernández has launched Sekondo, a plugin that connects ChatGPT and Claude to six Adobe applications: After Effects, Premiere Pro, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Lightroom Classic. Instead of generating new images or clips, the AI w...
entry.content:
Córdoba-based graphic designer Jose Manuel Fernández has launched Sekondo, a plugin that connects ChatGPT and Claude to six Adobe applications: After Effects, Premiere Pro, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Lightroom Classic.

Instead of generating new images or clips, the AI works inside the artist’s own project. You describe what you need, typed or spoken, and it applies the changes to your layers, keyframes, compositions and timelines, with everything left editable.
Like at any studio, a good part of Fernández’s day went into repetitive work: adapting a piece to twenty formats, versioning, building the same lower thirds again and again.

“These tasks are necessary, but they eat up hours I’d rather spend thinking up an idea. I built Sekondo to have more time to design.”

In Premiere Pro and After Effects, Sekondo can edit, animate and finish complete pieces with the artist’s own footage and under their direction, from the first cut to complex motion. Rather than handing back a finished clip that can’t be changed, it reads how a project is built, measures before it acts and keeps every layer editable.
The artist decides how far it goes: carrying out instructions, suggesting ideas and options, or building a whole piece from their idea. Files never leave the user’s computer.

Sekondo is published on Adobe Exchange, Adobe’s official marketplace for these apps, after passing Adobe’s review. It runs on macOS and Windows with the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps.

entry.title: ROVE Launches a New Identity and Website, Signs Ashley McKim Consulting
entry.summary: ROVE has launched a new brand identity and website, reflecting its evolution from a two-person live-action shop into a design, animation and motion-led creative studio. The launch also marks its signing with Ashley McKim Consulting for strategic sales and marketing across brands ...
entry.content:
ROVE has launched a new brand identity and website, reflecting its evolution from a two-person live-action shop into a design, animation and motion-led creative studio. The launch also marks its signing with Ashley McKim Consulting for strategic sales and marketing across brands and agencies.

Founded in Portland, Maine, in 2017 by Gabe Bornstein and Jay Brown, ROVE now works with a remote team across the U.S. and Canada. The name stays ROVE; “Beyond” expresses the studio’s approach to moving between disciplines, from design and animation to live action, VFX and production.

“We’ve grown into a studio driven by design and animation, and it was time for our brand to tell that story,” says Brown. “We don’t want to be defined by a single style or discipline.”

Built in partnership with STOKT, the website brings together a new showreel and expanded case studies for clients including Google, NOBULL and Spotify. Projects open up the studio’s process across design, animation, live action and finishing, while playful details extend to an interactive mini-game on the 404 page.

ROVE’s in-house creative team led the rebrand, working with a wider group of collaborators. Irene Feleo collaborated on the wordmark and core stamp, with other artists contributing their own stamp interpretations. Connor Linde contributed to elements of the brand identity. The studio carried the system through its website art direction, motion identity, showreel and presentation materials.

Ashley McKim Consulting joins ROVE’s existing representation by Aspire Artists Agency, which continues to focus on broadcast and streaming entertainment. ROVE’s work in that space includes Disney and Freeform’s 25 Days of Christmas. The studio’s broader client list includes Toyota, Converse and NOBULL.

FutureDeluxe takes Ferrari from the racetrack to the water in Hypersail, the official livery launch film created for Milan Design Week 2026.

Working directly with Ferrari before the vessel was built, the studio developed its materials, textures and livery in close collaboration with the client. The film turns advanced foil technology and integrated solar energy into a cinematic study of surface, light and engineering.

Scale provides the connection between two worlds. A Ferrari WEC car sits beneath the towering vessel, making Hypersail’s dimensions tangible while linking its design to Ferrari’s motorsport heritage.

The edit moves between rapid bursts and longer, controlled views. That contrast gives the film its momentum, pairing precise detail with a sense of speed. Audio is by group-project, with grading by Alex Gregory at Harbor.

Art&Graft brings a vivid, painterly world to What Is Dyslexia?, a short film directed by Kyra Bartley for Made By Dyslexia. Created with Clemenger BBDO and FINCH, it sets out to change what children and parents encounter when they search for dyslexia online.

The story follows Lola as she looks for answers and finds descriptions that make her future feel smaller. An unexpected guide opens a different path, taking her through encounters with invention, sport and storytelling that reveal a world of possibilities.

Art&Graft combines expressive brushwork and varied frame rates with 3D character animation. Hand-drawn marks move through the rendered world, giving the characters and environments a tactile, restless energy that carries Lola’s changing perspective.

entry.title: Creative Must Win: The Belief Behind RevThink’s Tim Thompson
entry.summary: Editor’s Note: In the years I’ve known Tim, he has become a dear friend, an advisor to Motionographer, and someone I feel lucky to have in my corner. We talk every week, and I rarely hang up without something new to think about: an insight that helps an idea take shape, a questio...
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: In the years I’ve known Tim, he has become a dear friend, an advisor to Motionographer, and someone I feel lucky to have in my corner. We talk every week, and I rarely hang up without something new to think about: an insight that helps an idea take shape, a question I hadn’t thought to ask, or a reminder that I don’t need to add one more thing to an already long list.

There is laughter, too. I love his sense of humor, and the kindness behind his support warms my heart. He makes me feel that the person carrying all those ideas matters as much as the ideas themselves.

I am mesmerized by the way his mind works. Tim has a gift for making complicated things feel clear while leaving you curious enough to keep exploring. At last week’s preview of Revolve, his new six-week accelerator for creative entrepreneurs, he held my attention for the entire hour.

When he finished, he asked the room whether he was onto something. That stayed with me. After giving us so much to think about, he still wanted to listen.

That combination of intelligence, humor, humility, and care is what I admire most about him. This piece is a love letter, and I’m happy to call it that. I adore Tim, I believe in the work he does, and I want more of our community to experience the generosity I get to feel in our conversations. I’ll be taking Revolve myself, because it is an experience not to be missed. You’ll find the details at the end.

Tim Thompson wanted to be a movie star.

Growing up in suburban Denver in the 1970s and ’80s, one of four brothers, he was the kid taking things apart and talking out of turn in class. On Saturday mornings, he watched That’s Hollywood. He wrote letters to television shows asking how things were made. Few wrote back.

His mother encouraged him. “I would share my plans with my mom, who supported me 1000%,” he says. With her help, he remembers screen-testing at seven for the role of Danny in Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining, without knowing what the story was about. He didn’t get the part, and it did little to shake his confidence: “I never doubted that I could build a successful career in entertainment.”

The part of that story he carries with him is his mother’s belief. “My mom believed in what I wanted to do and helped me pursue it,” he says. “These days, I get to offer that same support to others who believe in their talent and are willing to do the work.” There is a whole life connecting those two sentences.

At twenty-five, Tim married Katie, whom he calls the love of his life. Her support made anything feel possible, and she has been his partner through every change since. Around the same time, he joined RGA/LA, which became Imaginary Forces. He spent six years working in main titles, visual effects, and commercial post production, solving the kinds of production challenges he had dreamed about as a boy watching television.

He had found his way into Hollywood. By thirty, though, he was looking further ahead. He noticed how few people over fifty he encountered in the industry unless they were executives or union members. He started thinking about how to build a career that could last.

At thirty-two, the question became more personal. “I needed a new center in my life,” he says. “I found Jesus and went to seminary.” While studying, he continued working with studios and found a home at Trailer Park, where he spent five years building and managing operations before and during the company’s acquisition.

When he completed his master’s degree, he left Trailer Park and started RevThink. He put the experience he had gained at RGA/LA, Imaginary Forces, yU+co, and Trailer Park to work helping friends and colleagues build their own companies. That change had a cost. “It meant letting go of the career I had imagined as a kid,” he says.

When we talked about it, he went further.

“I would have never done this if it wasn’t for quitting who I thought I was becoming and becoming the person I needed to be.”

It is a significant thing to say after reaching the world you dreamed of entering. It also helps explain why he understands the difficulty of asking someone else to reconsider their future. What RevThink gave him was the opportunity to stay close to the work while helping owners through difficult decisions. Their relationships and accomplishments became the most meaningful part of his career.

Katie and Tim now travel together, visiting studios and agencies, speaking at conferences, and working with teams in person. They have built a life around their work, their relationships, and seeing the world together. They also have five sons and three grandsons. There is plenty of life beyond the next project.

That matters when you understand what Tim wants a business to make possible. When RevThink began, he saw a growing need for support that understood creative businesses from the inside. The tools of Motion Design and post production had become more accessible. Studios were appearing everywhere, and he was concerned about who would get to lead them.

He was seeing more companies started by people from sales and production, and fewer by creatives. “I thought we would gut our industry if we made it all about money,” he says. “Above everything else, I had learned one thing: ‘Creative Must Win.’” He wanted creative entrepreneurs to have the business support to build viable companies, lead their industry, and make the work they believed in.

He acknowledges the people who were already advising owners. Keir McLaren was working with Chris Do at Blind. Mike Simonoff was advising The Ebeling Group, Tim’s first client. Tim credits Simonoff with teaching him a great deal and giving him room to disagree.

What Tim brought was his experience inside creative production, and a desire to make that kind of support available more broadly. The name he chose describes the work. A revolution is a time of change; thinking is about strategy. Helping people through change became Revolution Thinking, and its shortened form, RevThink, also carries a nod to his seminary training and ordination.

Sometimes an owner comes to him when the situation is already severe. Tim describes employees walking out because payroll hasn’t been paid, or a project so far over budget that the owner doubts the company will survive. Often, though, it begins with loneliness.

A business grows. Decisions arrive faster. The owner reaches the limit of what they can carry, and the company stalls or begins to suffer from rushed choices. Tim starts by trying to understand the owner, the business, its clients, and the reason behind the work.

“You bring the compass,” he says. “I’ll build the roadmap.” Through his Seven Ingredients framework, that work becomes strategy, systems, routines, and people who can carry those practices forward. The company develops the ability to operate beyond its owner’s individual capacity.

But when I ask what makes him proudest, he describes the moment something clicks. An owner sees possibilities they had stopped considering. They recognize that they have the freedom to shape their career, and that some of the limits they have accepted can change.

One owner described it to him as “cataract surgery for a business.” Tim has his own name for it: “I call it ‘permission granted.’ It’s the best part of the job.”

His mother gave him encouragement to pursue a life he could imagine. Later, he had to give himself permission to change that life. Now he helps other people recognize that they have choices, too.

“I think people hear ‘business consultant’ and assume I’m mostly interested in the numbers,” he says. “I’ve spent my life around creative people, and I care deeply about what they make and what it takes out of them. I want the business to support that talent. When I push an owner on pricing, operations, or a difficult decision, it’s because I want them to keep doing meaningful work without sacrificing their health, their family, or their future.”

That concern now runs through his thinking about AI. Tim uses it himself to develop ideas, research, and write formulas that would otherwise take considerable trial and error. He also wishes it were better at editing without flattening different voices toward the same center. He has a name for a problem creative people are facing: the mastery paradox.

“A polished result can arrive before the understanding needed to judge it,” he writes. “That’s the paradox. You can produce something impressive without knowing why it works, where it fails, or how to improve it.”

An experienced artist’s value becomes visible when a decision has to be made. Does the work serve the story? Is the timing right? What happens when the client asks for a change?

“Being able to explain and deliberately improve the work matters more as generating options becomes easier,” he writes. For young artists, he emphasizes making choices, getting feedback, and revising. Developing judgment still requires experience, and he believes the people running studios have a responsibility to help create it.

“If we automate the work people used to learn from, we have to be intentional about creating new ways for them to develop judgment.”

During the Revolve preview, Tim asked us to examine the habits we repeat because they worked before. The portfolio, the reel, the website, the ways we find and maintain relationships with clients. Which assumptions are we still testing? Which have simply become routine?

He describes technological change as moving through revelation, revolution, and evolution. In his view, we are in the middle stage, still discovering what these tools make possible and what they mean for our businesses. Revolve is built around working through that uncertainty.

One exercise asks us to consider three questions: What did we think clients were buying? What might they actually value? How could we test the difference?

A client asks for a website. We understand the deliverable and begin thinking about how to make it. But what does the client need that website to accomplish? How will they judge whether it has worked?

Asking can change the conversation around the project. Tim brought it back to a question I think every creative entrepreneur should spend time with.

“What are clients paying us to understand, decide, and make possible?”

In his written answers, he suggests starting with a recent project. Ask the team what they understood that the client could not yet see, and which decisions the client trusted them to make. Those moments offer evidence of value that might never appear in a list of deliverables.

Over six weeks, Revolve gives participants time to examine those questions with other creative entrepreneurs. The process moves through assumptions about the future, expertise, client hesitation, and the possibility of developing new offerings, before connecting what the group has learned. Tim wants people to stay with difficult questions long enough to discover something. He expects some discomfort, and he expects participants to learn from one another, using the group to challenge the thinking they might otherwise keep repeating alone.

When I asked what success would look like for someone finishing the program, he returned to the same two words.

Permission granted.

He hopes someone will see a possibility they could not see before, feel less burdened by preserving a business exactly as it has always been, and become curious about what they could build next. The invitation extends to creative entrepreneurs, including freelancers thinking seriously about their businesses and their futures. As Tim and I discussed, the responsibilities of a freelancer and a studio owner can differ, while both have something to contribute to the conversation.

And because a life contains more than the questions that occupy our working days, I asked Tim a few quick ones.

The first thing you do in the morning?
Read the New York Times.

The music playing when you think best?
’80s pop. It gives me energy.

A piece of Motion Design you never tire of?
I’m a main title junkie. If you go to the movies with me, be ready for me to watch the entire end crawl.

A place that resets you?
The beach.

What makes you feel like a beginner again?
Technology always makes me restart. As I say, “Technology Follows Technique.”

The question you wish more studio owners asked you?
Am I trying to solve the wrong problem?

I love that he still stays for the end crawl. After all the changes in his life and career, the curiosity that sent those letters to Hollywood is still there. I also love that, when he talks about what he has accomplished, he keeps coming back to other people finding their way.

That is why I wanted to write this piece, and why I will be taking the full six weeks of Revolve myself. I attended the preview and found myself considering how these questions apply to Motionographer, to the people who trust us, and to the value we bring to our community. Tim made the conversation relevant to my own responsibilities, and I encourage you to experience it for yourself.

If you are a creative entrepreneur working through what this moment means for your business, bring a real question and join him. Revolve’s free kickoff sessions are on Tuesday, October 13, and Thursday, October 15, at 9 AM Pacific / noon Eastern. Just register on the program page, and the calendar invitation will follow.

The full six-week accelerator meets live online on Tuesdays and costs $1,500, with scholarships available upon request. Space is limited. Sessions are recorded, and participants have a shared online space to continue the conversation. If the cost is an obstacle, ask RevThink about available payment arrangements. An in-person gathering is also planned, with details to be confirmed.

Explore Revolve and sign up →

Thank you, Tim, for being in our corner.

I asked him what one sentence he wanted readers to remember.

“You don’t have to predict the future to take responsibility for your place in it.”

entry.content:

Anna Huijun Wang follows an identity from nothing to everything and back in OROBORO. Born as a single eye in cel animation, the character twists and morphs into a world of 2D Motion Design.

She gains limbs and geometry as the information around her accelerates. Each new dimension brings more of the world into her form, moving the film from hand-drawn animation through flat graphics and into 3D.

Immersed in social media and products, she becomes overwhelmed by the speed of the modern world. She begins to glitch and shed her dimensions, retracing her transformation toward the eye she began as.

For Wang, the changing mediums are states of being. The character’s journey gives shape to the weight of accumulating an identity and the act of letting it go. Created as her thesis film at USC’s Hench Division of Animation & Digital Arts, OROBORO features design by Matthew Sorgie and music and sound by Penrose Audio.

Inside a miniature workshop, a team of small, apron-wearing artisans gets to work. Chris Ullens turns the making of Diptyque’s wax Médicis vase into a stop-motion film, following the process through a world of curved workbenches, tiny tools and softly lit arches.

Commissioned by Diptyque, Ullens developed the concept, directed the film and animated its characters. The warm, restrained palette keeps the workers’ gestures in focus as they pour wax into molds and attend to the finished vases. A full-size candle beside the bench makes the scale of their world clear.

entry.content:
Monumental FX, the Paris-based visual effects and 3D animation studio, has established a US presence through a non-exclusive partnership with Modern Post. Announced on September 21, the agreement gives Monumental a US home base, with Modern Post providing local workflow, project management and finishing support for its American clients and agencies.

For Modern Post, the arrangement expands the visual effects resources it can bring to projects alongside its editing, color and finishing services. For Monumental, it creates a local point of contact for US filmmakers, brands and agencies working with its Paris team.

Monumental’s side of the partnership is led by co-founder Germain Robin, VFX creative director Mathieu Jussreandot and head of post-production Zoé Deurloo-Maka. Deurloo-Maka oversees the Paris VFX team and serves as a US-facing contact. Modern Post managing partner and executive producer Charlyn Derrick oversees the relationship with support from a dedicated US team.

“There’s a lot of creative crossover between our two companies,” says Derrick, describing the partnership as an extension of their work together.

Robin says the aim is to make working with Monumental as straightforward for American collaborators as working with a local studio. Founded in 2021, Monumental’s recent US-facing credits include Nike, Apple, Epic Games’ Fortnite Festival and Madonna.

Brooklyn filmmaker Anthony Koithra’s debut original animated short, Machines Learning, premieres this October at NYC Indie Shorts Awards, Newport Beach Film Festival, and the Oscar-qualifying San Jose International Short Film Festival. The darkly comic film follows a bullying factory worker whose robots observe his behavior, learn from it, and eventually turn on him. It asks a timely question: if our machines are learning, what are we teaching them?

Created almost entirely solo over two years, apart from an original score by Tyson Cazier, the eight-minute film turns anxieties about AI, labor, and power into a mechanical uprising culminating in a giant kaiju robot chase. Koithra wrote, directed, and animated the film, working primarily in Unreal Engine.

entry.title: AI Animation, IP and the Next Phase of Creative Production
entry.summary: Generative AI is rapidly moving from experimentation into professional animation and commercial production. For studios, agencies and brands, the opportunity is significant. Work that once required lengthy technical processes can now be explored, developed and refined in entirely...
entry.content:
Generative AI is rapidly moving from experimentation into professional animation and commercial production. For studios, agencies and brands, the opportunity is significant. Work that once required lengthy technical processes can now be explored, developed and refined in entirely new ways.

But as AI becomes part of mainstream production, a more important question is emerging: what happens to the material being put into these systems?

Creative teams routinely work with unreleased campaigns, proprietary characters, product designs, confidential footage and valuable client intellectual property (IP). Uploading those assets to a generative platform is therefore very different from experimenting with a public prompt.

Yet protections vary considerably between AI providers. Some platforms explicitly commit not to train models on customer content, particularly under enterprise agreements. Others retain broad rights over uploaded material or use information generated through user interactions to improve and train their systems.

For businesses, a privacy setting or the ability to keep an output hidden is not necessarily the same thing as guaranteeing that underlying data cannot contribute to model development.

Jon Draper, Creative Director for Generative AI at Synima and founder of AIAnimation.com, believes this will become one of the defining issues as AI animation matures.

The next stage of AI production will not simply be about generating better images. It will be about building professional infrastructure around those models, with clear ownership, controlled access, secure handling of client assets, traceable workflows and transparency over how data is used.

As generative animation moves into serious commercial production, creative capability and IP security can no longer be treated as separate conversations.

entry.title: Bayeux Tapestry Comes to Life | Hocus Pocus Studio
entry.summary: The Bayeux Tapestry arrived in the UK in September, on display at the British Museum for the first time in almost a thousand years. Ahead of what became the most in-demand exhibition in the Museum’s history, the British Museum commissioned Hocus Pocus Studio to make three animate...
entry.content:
The Bayeux Tapestry arrived in the UK in September, on display at the British Museum for the first time in almost a thousand years. Ahead of what became the most in-demand exhibition in the Museum’s history, the British Museum commissioned Hocus Pocus Studio to make three animated short films for its learning programme.
The films are built primarily for secondary school audiences aged 11 to 14, but with enough charm and depth for a much broader audience. Each runs two to three minutes, and they are being released in sequence. The first two are live now: How is the Bayeux Tapestry still here after 1000 years? and What’s the story in the Bayeux Tapestry?

The first animation starts with the Tapestry itself. Figures and scenes are lifted directly from the embroidery and set in motion. Where the Tapestry has gaps, hand-drawn animation fills them, matched closely enough that the join isn’t visible. Art Director Theresa Hilsden describes the challenge as staying as faithful as possible to the original while still finding room for the humour the films needed.
The series doesn’t just retell 1066. The second film uses the Tapestry to make a sharper point: historical sources aren’t neutral. Of the four men who claimed the English throne that year, only Harold and William appear in any depth, while Hardrada and Edgar are almost entirely written out. The films treat that absence as evidence, asking audiences who made the Tapestry, and for whom.

entry.title: STUDIO STORIES: Tonic DNA, The Studio That Refused to Be One Thing
entry.summary: Editor’s Note: This Studio Story was reported the way most of our lives now happen: on a screen, between New York and Montreal. One long conversation over Zoom at the end of August, recorded, followed by a written questionnaire that Stefanie Bitton answered in her own voice and a...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player

Editor’s Note:

This Studio Story was reported the way most of our lives now happen: on a screen, between New York and Montreal. One long conversation over Zoom at the end of August, recorded, followed by a written questionnaire that Stefanie Bitton answered in her own voice and at her own pace over the weeks that followed. I had cancelled on her twice. When we finally spoke I was running on cold medicine, she was running a studio, and neither of us was willing to cancel a third time.

I am glad we did not, because what came through that screen was not a pitch. It was a partner who has spent twenty years inside a studio twice that old, talking about drawings, phone calls, a beaver, a penguin-powered Santa and the people at the desks, with the same steadiness whether the subject was an Oscar or a spreadsheet.

What I did not expect was the candor. Twice in that hour she corrected my premise without apology: no, this is a refresh, not a rebrand, and no, 2D never went anywhere, so there is nothing to bring back. When she did not have an answer she said so, and when we reached the film that still makes her cry she let the pause do the talking. A partner with four decades of studio history behind her and nothing to oversell is a rare interview, and it made this piece a pleasure to write.

We held the story until Tonic’s new website went live. The refresh is the doorway into this piece, and a doorway needs a house behind it. What follows is not a profile of a studio. It is an argument that a company can change its tools, its model and even its name, and remain unmistakably itself, as long as it protects two things: the people and the standard.

It arrives in the month Motionographer turns twenty, about a studio that has been at this for twice as long. I find that comforting. Someone has already walked the road ahead, and they are still walking.

This month, Tonic DNA turned on a new website. The wordmark is spare: TONIC in wide, quiet capitals, dna underneath in lowercase, warm cream on near black, with a jolt of sage green where the studio wants your eye. It is the kind of change a company might be tempted to call a rebrand. Stefanie Bitton will not.

“I call it a refresh more than a rebrand. A rebrand is when a company is changing more than the visual of their logo and their website. They are becoming something new, something different. We are not changing how we operate. We are not changing our model. This is a refresh of our visual guidelines.”

The distinction matters to her because Tonic DNA has already lived through the other kind, and the difference between the two is the whole story of the studio. Tonic DNA is a Montreal studio with roots reaching back about forty years, three or four buildings ago, always downtown. In that time it has been a traditional animation house, an IMAX pioneer, a 3D and hybrid shop, a director-led creative studio, and now a company with an original property in production and an AI pipeline built by its own artists. The thread running through all of it is not a look.

“It’s the refusal to let animation stand still. That’s been part of the studio from the beginning.”

A name that is a job description

Ask what people remembered about the studio for decades and the answer arrives quickly: an Academy Award. The Old Man and the Sea, Alexander Petrov’s adaptation of the Hemingway novella, was painted in oil on glass, frame by frame, and produced for IMAX, which had never been attempted with an animated film. It won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film in 2000. “They had created this new kind of camera. Everything about that film was innovative,” Bitton says.

She was not there when the statue came home, but she has watched what it did to the studio’s name ever since. “When everybody would hear our name, they would remember that,” she says. Bernard Lajoie, a founder who remains one of her two partners, is the through line. He produced the IMAX film, then brought 3D into a house built on drawing.

“He’s one of the pioneers when it comes to innovation and technology,” Bitton says. “He’s lived through these transitions, 2D technology, 3D technology. This is something he’s proud of.” The real rebrand came in 2017, when the studio took the Tonic DNA name and, more importantly, a new shape.

“Before, we were a craft studio under one creative vision. Now we’re going towards a director-led vision, where multiple directors lead the creative, and we’re really putting the emphasis on the artists. That was a complete shift. It was a change from what we had been doing the previous twenty years to how we wanted to move forward for the following twenty.”

The name was chosen to sound like what it was for. Tonic, because the partners wanted something energizing and revitalizing, a fresh start with a new model. DNA, because it stood for directors and animators, the people the model was built around. It has since stretched to hold designers and artists, and lately developers and AI, three strands the studio is deliberately growing. The name is a job description that keeps getting longer.

Story first, technique second

“Tonic DNA was built on a simple belief,” Bitton says. “Animation is a storytelling medium, not a technique.” The style comes from what the idea needs, which is why the studio’s identity does not live in a signature look, and why its directors can sound nothing like one another.

“The common thread is that the director leads the vision, the animators shape the performance, and everyone is working in service of the story. That’s where the identity of the studio lives for me.”

It is also why the studio almost never changes technique mid-flight. Pre-production at Tonic is long on purpose, so that every stakeholder understands the designs, the characters and the story before a frame is animated. “Once we release it for production, it’s no longer a surprise,” Bitton says. “They already know what to expect.”

Where the studio does switch techniques is on itself. Jump is an internal research project built around a single character, remade year after year to test tools. One year it was 3D animation dressed in 2D textures and lighting. The next, the same character came back with hyper-realistic surfaces and a first round of AI tools. It is the refusal to be one thing, made literal.

Drawing for people who already know the character

Tonic’s hand-drawn work has been part of 2D animation’s renewed visibility on the big screen, from The Bob’s Burgers Movie to Disenchanted to The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie. Ask Bitton whether that amounts to a renaissance and she rejects the premise.

“A renaissance suggests 2D disappeared. It never did. It’s the foundational form of animation, and there’s something enduring about drawing and bringing those drawings to life that I think will always have a place. What has changed is everything around the craft.”

Animating a character the audience already knows by heart is its own discipline. “First of all, the love of the character,” she says. “A clear understanding of who that character is, what is his personality, how he moves, his history, where he is going. When you say, please animate Bugs Bunny, we have a really good understanding of Bugs Bunny’s character and how he moves and who he is. That is not a simple request for other animators.”

The same care goes into work that never leaves Quebec. The IGA holiday tale is a local tradition now, written and produced entirely by Quebec talent with agency Sid Lee, and Tonic has animated three installments: The Meatloaf in 2022, Mr. Beaver’s Yule Log in 2023 and Paulo’s Wish in 2024. For Mr. Beaver’s Yule Log, directors Kun Chang and Fabien Fulchiron built the story world out of plush children’s toys, CG characters with touch-worn textures and a stop-motion feel, framed as a grandfather’s bedtime tale about a grumpy beaver who learns to share. “Every year it’s such a beautiful story, so beautifully crafted and animated,” Bitton says. “It’s very much part of our Quebec culture, and for us it was so exciting to get the opportunity to produce three of them.”

(un)Hungry, made for the American insurer Highmark’s campaign against food insecurity, is the studio’s CG work at its most handmade. Directors Jamil Lahham and Fabien Fulchiron gave the film a painterly, stop-motion sensibility, painting the characters’ hair in virtual reality and adding brush strokes by hand to the 3D sets, for a story about one little girl’s quest to help that was inspired by a real neighborhood pantry. Fulchiron also co-directed Mr. Beaver’s Yule Log and Paulo’s Wish. The film took a MUSE Platinum this year.

Asked which piece she would run back into a burning building to save, she does not hesitate. Freebird is a five-minute short made for L’Arche Canada that follows forty-five years in the life of a man with Down syndrome, made on a limited budget and a tight schedule. “The creative was just amazing, and the final result, every time I see it,” she says, trailing off.

“Those are my favorite projects, the ones that get me emotional when I look at them. I start tearing up and I think, this project is just too good. Why is this doing this to me?”

The people behind that range are the point. Malcolm Sutherland has directed at the studio for about a decade and is, in Bitton’s telling, the desk you cannot walk past. “He’s constantly reinventing himself, using new tools, developing new styles, coming up with new original content,” she says. “Every time I sit in front of his desk, he has something fun and new to look at.”

Learning animation by selling it

Bitton did not come to animation as an animator. She studied marketing and international business, did an internship in Costa Rica, and came home with Spanish and a sales instinct. In 2005 the studio was looking for someone to develop Latin America from nothing, and she took the job. “My first six months was learn animation,” she says. “What is 2D animation, what is 3D animation, and then learn the business. How do production companies work with advertising agencies and clients? What are the services we’re offering?”

Then she picked up the phone. “I did it the old-fashioned way,” she says. “I would give a call and introduce myself, and the person on the other end of the line was so happy. One, I was from Montreal. Two, I was trying to speak Spanish to them.” Mexico and Colombia were her first markets, and Mexico City taught her a lesson she still runs the studio by: relationships are key. From there came the U.S. Hispanic market, then Europe and Africa.

Partnership followed the growth. The sales she was bringing in were building the studio, so the owners asked her to join them, and she has been a partner ever since. She describes the road from producer to leader to owner as something closer to weather than to milestones.

“There wasn’t one dramatic moment where everything changed. It was more a series of small shifts in responsibility. By the time I looked up, I was already doing the next version of the job.”

What the refresh is for

Under the new mark, the studio runs on two divisions, short form for advertising, branding, content and music videos, and long form for series and features. This year it added a third. Tonic DNA’s latest original property, The Anta Claus of the South Pole, is a 24-minute 2D holiday special directed by Cordell Barker, the two-time Oscar nominee behind The Cat Came Back and Strange Invaders. It is a co-production with the National Film Board of Canada, the studio’s first, made in association with Crave, a division of Bell Media, with the participation of the Canada Media Fund, and it is planned for release this year.

Envious of his northern counterpart, the Anta Claus sets off on a penguin-powered journey to find the secret of a flawless Christmas, and learns that the holiday lives in the community of oddballs he left behind. “It’s been quietly sitting with us for more than fifteen years, so finally bringing it into production feels really special,” Bitton says. She does not see it as a turn away from client work.

“We’ve spent decades helping other people bring their characters and stories to life, and we’re very proud of that work. But there’s also something incredibly rewarding about developing and nurturing an idea that originates inside the studio. I don’t think those two sides compete. If anything, they strengthen one another.”

The fourth strand is the one everyone asks about. Tonic has spent two years building its own AI tools, and Bitton calls the approach AI with intention. “One of the biggest changes is how much more we can explore before committing to a direction,” she says. “That doesn’t mean replacing the artist or skipping the craft. It means removing some of the friction around the process so the artists have more room to experiment.” The target is long-form 2D, where the tools let a project attempt ideas that would once have been too slow or too risky for the schedule.

The artists were not sold on day one. “At first there was a lot of resistance,” she says. “But because we’ve been developing our own internal tools, and the artists have all been involved in the development, it’s something they accept. They actually enjoy it, because it’s helping with their own workload.” Her line in the sand is transparency.

“Artists need to understand what tools are being used, how they’re being used, and what that means for their work. Once the technology starts obscuring authorship or bypassing consent, you’ve crossed into a very different territory.”

Independence is what makes that kind of choice possible. Tonic DNA has never belonged to a larger group, and Bitton is clear about what that buys. “Flexibility, and being able to try new things,” she says. “Making new mistakes, learning from them, and evolving into what we choose to be, as opposed to someone else.”

The wall in 2033

In seven years the studio turns fifty, and Bitton already knows what will be on the wall at the party. Not the reel, not the trophies: a slideshow of everyone who has worked there, some of them for twenty and thirty years and still on the floor. Asked to picture the celebration, she filled the room with faces.

That is the refresh, in the end. A new logo, new colors, a new voice and a new site, wrapped around a studio that changed its model once, its tools many times, and its DNA never. Motionographer turns twenty this month. Tonic DNA is twice that, and by its own account only getting started. “We all need to figure it out,” Bitton says. “We all need to reinvent ourselves, because the whole landscape is changing. This is just the beginning.”

Ask her to finish the sentence “Animation will survive every technological disruption because,” and she answers without pause.

“Because the people who make it and the people who love it believe in it.”

The Tonic DNA Rapid Fire

  • Refresh or rebrand: “A refresh. We’re not changing how we operate.”
  • What DNA stands for: “Directors and animators. Now designers and artists, and developers and AI.”
  • The piece she would run into a burning building for: Freebird. “Every time I see it.”
  • What Mexico City taught her: “Relationships are key.”
  • The desk you cannot walk past: Malcolm Sutherland’s. “He’s always doing something different.”
  • Advice to a twenty-year-old animation student: “Love animation fully. We’re the biggest fans of animation.”
  • What being independent buys: “Evolving into what we choose to be.”
  • On the wall at the fiftieth, in 2033: “A slideshow of all the people who have worked with us.”
  • What she hopes readers feel: “Impressed with what we’ve accomplished, and excited about what’s coming.”

entry.title: Dear Upstairs Neighbors: How Connie He Taught a Machine to See the Way She Draws.
entry.summary: Pixar alum Connie He on turning insomnia into a six-minute short, tuning a model to her own concept art, and what it took for animators and researchers to speak the same language. Editor’s note: Dear Upstairs Neighbors had its world premiere as part of Whoopi’s Wonderful World of...
entry.content:
▶ Ver video / Watch on external player




Pixar alum Connie He on turning insomnia into a six-minute short, tuning a model to her own concept art, and what it took for animators and researchers to speak the same language.

Editor’s note: Dear Upstairs Neighbors had its world premiere as part of Whoopi’s Wonderful World of Animation at the 2026 Tribeca Festival. Motionographer was in the theater for every short in the program, and this article is part of our series dedicated to the films of this year’s lineup, with more on the way.

Dear Upstairs Neighbors. Courtesy of the filmmakers

Somewhere in the middle of our conversation, Connie He stopped explaining how she conceived and directed Dear Upstairs Neighbors and started marveling at it, as if she were discovering the film for the first time. She was describing the earliest tests she and her team ran on a video model trained on their own concept art. The model picked up a low camera angle nobody had asked for. It picked up the zigzag lines the team drew wherever an object touched the ground, and nobody had told it those lines mattered.

“We’re like, oh my god, it’s picking up on all those patterns that we didn’t even think of. That’s kind of an aha moment. We’re like, okay, I think what we are thinking is actually possible.”

More than anything else she told me, that moment holds the essence of Dear Upstairs Neighbors, the six-minute animated short that previewed at Sundance in January, had its world premiere at the Tribeca Festival in June, and went on to SIGGRAPH in July. The film follows Ada, a woman who cannot sleep because of the noise coming from the apartment above her. The racket summons hallucinations, beautiful and increasingly unhinged, that attack her exhausted mind.

Ada, before the night begins. Courtesy of the filmmakers

But this funny, colorful, kinetic film is also a document of two worlds learning to talk to each other: artists and machine learning researchers. And it is a rare thing, an account from inside the process of what generative tools might be for, delivered by someone who is still not sure of the answer.

A word first about who made it, because our readers will ask. Dear Upstairs Neighbors is a Google DeepMind production. Connie and her producer, Márcia Mayer, worked alongside a team of DeepMind researchers and engineers, with Doug Eck, Glenn Entis, and David Salesin as executive producers, and the film’s look was built on custom versions of Google’s Veo and Imagen models fine-tuned on the film’s own concept art. Google has been open about all of this and has published its own account of the production. What follows is Connie’s, and she does not pretend the divide over any of it is not real.

Full insomnia, zero ambition

The short did not begin as a bid to make a prestigious animated piece that would shape the future of Motion Design. It began, Connie said, with real sleepless nights during the pandemic. “It was always started as like a personal expression,” she told me. “I never really thought it would actually become a short film. It was just like, I was so frustrated, and I feel like I have a lot of emotion, I need to put it out.”

One weekend, Connie went to a coffeehouse, wrote her feelings down on paper, and started the first version of what would become Dear Upstairs Neighbors. She got a storyboard about 80 percent of the way there. Then she left it alone for a long time.

The board came back to life when Connie and some friends from her Pixar days started talking about what machine learning might mean for artists. They were curious and cautious in equal measure, so they decided to understand the process by testing it on a story. Connie already had one sitting around, nearly finished, and it became the test bed.

I think a lot about this origin story, because it contradicts two easy narratives circulating about AI and animation. This is not a director chasing a trend. And this is not a tool inventing a film out of nothing. Dear Upstairs Neighbors was born from something that happened to a person who needed to get it out of her body, and who happened to be standing there when a new kind of paintbrush became available.

A bedroom and an anger taken from life

One of the pleasures of the film is Ada’s bedroom. It is full of books and small objects that seem to tell their own story. I told Connie the bedroom was one of my favorite things in the short, and her answer surprised me. She had asked her production designer, fellow Pixar alum Yingzong Xin, to put her own home into it.

“When we talk about, what do we design for Ada, I was like, Yingzong, how about you just design, put your own bedroom, put your own home into the design. A lot of the objects in the room is actual stuff that she has in her room and living room. If you get a chance to go to her place, you’ll see all the bookshelves, all the small details. I think those are the stuff to make her living room feel relatable, because they are real.”

That is the whole philosophy behind the production design, and it happened before any generative tool touched the film. Connie and Yingzong built a real, emotional imprint with traditional means: references, taste, and the stubborn textures of an actual apartment.

The anger came from life too. Connie grew up around the abstract art her father made, and she wanted to see whether that kind of work could carry a story.

“You seldom see that kind of artwork appear in animation or filmmaking, so I thought maybe that’s an interesting experiment, to see if we can bring those expressionistic ways into visual storytelling. That’s kind of where I set the art direction. I wanted to experiment. I think about Jackson Pollock’s art. I think that’s a great representation for expressing intense emotion, like anger. So I thought it’d be cool to add that. For the mood board, I brought in a lot of super abstract painting. I didn’t have a very clear idea of how I could visualize it, but that’s what I wanted to feel.”

Ada, past the point of patience. Courtesy of the filmmakers

An instrument to be tuned, not a button to be pressed

The most quietly remarkable thing about the film is that the tool was treated as an instrument to be tuned, not a button to be pressed. Connie and her team joined a group of researchers and engineers at Google DeepMind and, with them, developed custom builds of the video model based on Connie and Yingzong’s own concept art. The starting material was small. “I think we actually fine-tuned about 12 concept art-ish with different layers broken down, so maybe hundreds of different images,” Connie explained.

That is where the moment at the top of this piece comes from. The model absorbed the low, two-point perspective they had used throughout their concept art without anyone flagging it as a rule. It absorbed the zigzag ground-contact lines, and it learned the brushstroke.

For the shots themselves, the team built tools for what Connie calls localized refinement: editing specific regions of a frame with adjustable control rather than regenerating a whole shot from scratch every time something needed a note. When I asked whether this changed her relationship to a shot compared with a traditional animation revision, her answer was almost anticlimactic in the best way. If you already know a CG pipeline, she told me, it did not feel like a rupture at all. She had worked on Inside Out 2 at Pixar and spent time as a CG generalist on the first season of Love, Death & Robots, working in compositing tools like Nuke, layering nodes and iterating until a picture looked right. The new workflow, she said, was the same thinking process wearing a different coat.

One of the hallucinations: the drill. Courtesy of the filmmakers

I find that reassuring in a way I did not expect. So much of the conversation around generative tools treats them as a total break from craft. Connie’s experience suggests something gentler and more useful to working animators: good judgment, honed over years of dailies and revisions and story notes, does not get replaced by new tools. It gets asked to do the same job in a new room.

Protecting the joke while the technology was still being invented

One of the things that struck me watching Dear Upstairs Neighbors is how funny it is. It is adorable, a little unhinged, and its comic timing lands cleanly, which is not a small thing to pull off while your production pipeline is being built in real time alongside the film. So I asked Connie how she protected the comedy through all that technical uncertainty.

Her answer was almost defiantly old-fashioned. The storytelling and the timing, she said, were mostly locked in the storyboard phase, long before any generative tool entered the process. Once the project came back to life, the board went through 27 versions over a year and a half, a side project she worked on with her producer, Márcia Mayer, and refined with editors brought in specifically to nail the rhythm of the story. “That’s probably a lot of pre-production, good pre-production, and working directly with editors and people who give story notes,” she said. “Then later on the production is just about executing. How do you execute to meet your creative vision.”

Ada versus the speaker. Courtesy of the filmmakers

It is a useful thing to hear right now, when it is easy to assume that generative workflows collapse the traditional stages of filmmaking into something faster and looser. In Connie’s account, they did not collapse anything. Pre-production still did what pre-production has always done. The new tools showed up later, in service of a vision that had already been earned the hard way.

Two worlds, one language

None of this happened without friction. When Connie and Márcia first joined the DeepMind team, there was a wide gap between what the artists wanted and what the researchers understood the work to require.

“We realized there’s a lot of gap between these two worlds and the language that we speak. So at first, we set up a lot of fun hackathons. And we invite people to say, hey, let’s just use one day or three hours. Let’s make a film together with our current toolings. And very quickly, all the researchers and people start to realize, oh, this is not how you can make a good film.”

From there, she said, the questions changed. What does a filmmaker actually want? What does a system built to support a vision look like? What is the creative process? “Clearly, you can’t just click a button to make a good film,” she said. “What does it take to make a good film? Let’s try to understand it.”

The night gets worse before it gets better. Courtesy of the filmmakers

“People keep saying like AI, it’s weird to put the AI, because it feels like a mysterious entity,” Connie noted. “But under the hood, what’s down to the essence, it’s machine learning. It’s about what you can teach the machine to learn.” She kept returning to a line she said gets repeated a lot at Pixar: art inspires technology, and technology inspires art. Her open question, and she was not being falsely modest when she called it open, is whether these tools end up as a way to make things faster and cheaper, or become something closer to a new medium, sitting alongside watercolor and oil paint and CG as one more way to tell a story.

I asked her about the sharp divide in our community over whether any of this belongs in animation at all, and about what happened at Annecy in June, when the world premiere of Hisko Hulsing’s Danse Macabre drew walkouts and boos over its use of generative tools. She did not flinch from the question, and she did not pretend the divide is not real.

“I think there’s a huge gap between what the technology is, what the technology can do, how people think it is, and inside the world of the people who are making the technology, their understanding of filmmaking and the creative process.”

Her instinct, and the more I sit with this film the more I share it, is that you cannot argue anyone into a position on this. You can only show the work, show how it was made, and let the conversation grow from there. “I really wish we can have more conversation between those two worlds, and even among artists ourselves,” she said. “I feel like the way that we make things on Dear Upstairs Neighbors is just one way it’s possible. It could be other ways, with other artists. But all those conversations need to happen first.”

What comes after

Connie is back in what she calls a learning and input phase, reading and researching new stories while she keeps an eye on how far the technology has come, trusting that the two will meet again somewhere down the line. After years in short-form storytelling, she is ready to think in a longer format. She asked me to wish her luck. I will, gladly, and so should you.

I keep thinking about the first time I watched this film at home, before I understood any of what had gone into it. I assumed I was watching a wonderful piece of hand-crafted animation, full stop. When I later learned about the AI collaboration behind it, my first instinct was suspicion. I have seen enough plastic, boring, soulless AI video by now to have a reflexive concern about the label.

Sleep, at last. Courtesy of the filmmakers

Dear Upstairs Neighbors is not that, and talking to Connie made it obvious why. The technology did not replace the person behind it. It learned, quite literally, to reproduce the way she already saw. That is the real story here, and the reason this film deserves to be more than a case study in how a research lab and a group of animators worked together. It is a reminder of what happens when the people building these tools are willing to sit in a room with artists long enough to listen.

Connie He did not just make a funny, gorgeous short about not being able to sleep. She made a small, hopeful proof that the future everyone is arguing about does not have to be a fight. It can be a conversation, patiently and stubbornly had, until both sides start speaking the same language.

Congratulations, Connie. Here’s to whatever keeps you up at night next.

entry.title: Who Moved My Work? Tim Thompson on RevThink’s The Weekly Briefing
entry.summary: AI didn’t arrive yesterday. Clients didn’t wake up this morning and decide they could do more themselves, and the value of creative work didn’t change overnight. But it is easy to get comfortable with where the work has always come from, what clients have always paid for, and wha...
entry.content:
AI didn’t arrive yesterday. Clients didn’t wake up this morning and decide they could do more themselves, and the value of creative work didn’t change overnight. But it is easy to get comfortable with where the work has always come from, what clients have always paid for, and what studios have always been hired to do. Until one day, you look up and the work has moved.
That is the question behind “Who Moved My Work?”, today’s edition of RevThink’s The Weekly Briefing with Tim Thompson. The live session looks at who thrives in a time of change and why some people get stuck waiting.

Thompson will cover how to recognize that the work is moving before it’s gone, what you may be holding onto simply because it worked before, and how to adapt strategically before the market forces you to. If the signals are already showing up in your pipeline, your client relationships, or the work you’re being asked to do, the question isn’t whether the market is changing. It’s whether you’re changing with it.

The session is live and open to everyone, today, Wednesday, September 23, at 5pm ET.

Motionographer turns 20 this year. Twenty years, no ads, no sponsors, one publication pointing at the work and the people who make it. We are not going to mark it with a retrospective. We are going to mark it the way this community marks anything worth marking: in a room, with the work on a wall and the people who made it standing in front of it.

It happens that the best room of the year lands in our city the same week. Motion Plus Design comes to New York on Saturday, September 26, and Motionographer is its media partner. So the 20th is a weekend, not a night.

Motion Plus Design New York, 2025. Photo: Motion Plus Design

Friday, September 25: Founder House, and 20 seats for 20 years

The night before the conference, the speakers and the people who built Motionographer gather on a private rooftop in Lower Manhattan. Eighty people. No tickets, no charge, projectors on the wall of the building next door, the work of this year’s Motion Awards winners on a loop. It is a birthday, not a bar.

Twenty of those seats belong to you, and the way in is a conference ticket. Every Motion Plus Design ticket bought by Wednesday, September 23 goes into a draw, run by Motion Plus Design from their own list, and twenty names come out. If you already bought one, you are in. Winners hear by email on Thursday, September 24, with the address. There is nothing to sign up for, no form, no follow. Buy the ticket, and on Thursday check your inbox.

Saturday, September 26: Motion Plus Design New York

One day, one stage, at Roulette in Brooklyn, 509 Atlantic Avenue, doors at 1pm. The lineup runs Mehdi Hadi, Saad Moosajee, Bhakti Patel, Danaé Gosset, Brian Yoo, Rachel Brickel and Vallée Duhamel, with Spenser Dickerson of Render Network and Áron Filkey of Runway on the tools side, and the closing at 7:15pm. Kook Ewo has spent fifteen years building this conference in Paris, Tokyo and Los Angeles as the rare event where the talks are about the craft, not the pitch, and last year he brought it to New York for the first time. This is the second edition, and the room is bigger. The full program is below, and the trailer above is the fastest way to understand why we said yes before we were asked.
